title: Synthesis of Mg-Al layered double hydroxides by electrocoagulation
author: Molano-Mendoza, Donneys-Victoria, et al.
materials: Synthesized LDHs were then characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), surface area analyses (BET) and Fourier-transformed infrared (FTIR). X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern were recorder using a X’pert PRO – PANalytical diffractometer under the following conditions: 45 kV, 40 mA, monochromatic CuKα radiation λ=0.1542 nm in the 2 θ range of 4°–90°. The FTIR spectra were recorder with a JASCO FT/IR-4100 in a range between 500–4000 cm−1;samples were prepared by mixing the powdered solids with KBr. Surface area and pore analysis were performed using the Brunauer-Emmet-Teller (BET) approach on a Micrometrics ASAP 2020 adsorption analyzer. Zeta potential was measured using a Zeta-Meter 4.0 (Malvern Instruments, Malvern, UK) at 25 °C in clear disposable zeta cells, the pH and conductivity was measured using a Thermo Scientific Orion multiparameter (Star A329).

steps.title: Assemble electrocoagulation reactor
steps.instruction: Set up a batch‑mode electrocoagulation cell using a 1 L glass reactor. Add 0.9 L of AR‑grade aqueous solution. Install two parallel electrode plates – one aluminum plate and one AZ31 magnesium alloy plate – each with an immersed surface area of 46.6 cm² and spaced 5 mm apart. Place a magnetic stirrer beneath the reactor and stir at 100 rpm. Connect the electrodes to a DC power supply and a manual polarity inverter, and set the current to 5 mA while maintaining room temperature (24–26 °C).

steps.title: Abrade and rinse electrodes
steps.instruction: Dry‑abrade each electrode first with emery paper No. 600, then with abrasive paper No. 1000. Rinse the electrodes with distilled water for approximately 5 minutes to remove metal residues.

steps.title: Choose experimental conditions
steps.instruction: Select the alternating polarity time and electrolyte‑pollutant concentration according to Table 1: use alternating polarity intervals of 8 min and 5 min; employ either a NaCl solution (200–1800 ppm Indigo carmine) or a NaCl solution (5000 ppm) as the electrolyte.

steps.title: Calculate charge and metal ratios
steps.instruction:
Determine the required electrical charge (Q) and the Mg²⁺/Al³⁺ (M²⁺/M³⁺) ratio using Faraday’s law:
Al (g L⁻¹) = I × t × M_Al / (F × V) = 3600 × Q × M_Al / F
Mg (g L⁻¹) = I × t × M_Mg / (F × V) = 3600 × Q × M_Mg / F
where I is current (A), t is time (s), M_Al = 26.98 g mol⁻¹, M_Mg = 24.305 g mol⁻¹, F = 96.485 C mol⁻¹, V is the initial volume (mL).

steps.title: Run electrocoagulation with polarity switching
steps.instruction: Start the EC process with the current set to 5 mA. Switch the polarity of the electrodes according to the chosen alternating times (e.g., 8 min on one polarity, then 5 min on the opposite polarity) and continue until the calculated charge Q is reached. Keep stirring at 100 rpm and monitor temperature (24–26 °C).

steps.title: Filter, dry and macerate product
steps.instruction: Immediately after the EC run, filter the suspension to collect the solid. Transfer the solid to a drying oven set at 105 °C and dry for 2 h. After drying, grind (macerate) the material to a fine powder for further analysis.

steps.title: Determine chlorine uptake by atomic absorption
steps.instruction: Take an aliquot of the post‑EC solution, add excess AgNO₃ to precipitate AgCl, and separate the solid. Measure the concentration of unreacted Ag⁺ using a Shimadzu AA‑7000 atomic‑absorption spectrophotometer. Calculate the amount of chlorine adsorbed on the solid from the stoichiometric difference before and after EC.

steps.title: Record X‑ray diffraction pattern
steps.instruction: Analyse the dried powder with a PANalytical X’pert PRO diffractometer under the following conditions: 45 kV, 40 mA, Cu Kα radiation (λ = 0.1542 nm), scanning 2θ from 4° to 90°. Identify peaks (e.g., 11.827°, 23.373°, 34.076°, 36.147°, 62.097°) and compare with JCPDS files 98‑000‑6183 (hydrotalcite) and 98‑003‑4961 (brucite).

steps.title: Collect FT‑IR spectra
steps.instruction: Prepare KBr pellets by mixing a small amount of the powdered sample with dry KBr. Record FT‑IR spectra on a JASCO FT/IR‑4100 in the range 500–4000 cm⁻¹. Note characteristic bands (e.g., 574 cm⁻¹ Al‑O, 3636 cm⁻¹ O‑H, 3565–3500 cm⁻¹ M‑OH, 1641 cm⁻¹ H₂O bending, 1069 cm⁻¹ carbonate).

steps.title: Measure BET surface area and porosity
steps.instruction: Determine specific surface area, pore volume and average pore size using a Micrometrics ASAP 2020 analyzer following the BET method. Record values (e.g., 220.0 m² g⁻¹, 0.008 cm³ g⁻¹, 64.4 Å for the Brucite sample; 206.3 m² g⁻¹, 0.359 cm³ g⁻¹, 69.6 Å for the hydrotalcite sample).

steps.title: Assess zeta potential, pH and conductivity
steps.instruction: Measure the zeta potential of a suspension of the product using a Malvern Zeta‑Meter 4.0 at 25 °C (e.g., +39 mV for Brucite, +30 mV for hydrotalcite). Simultaneously record pH (6.5–10.5 for Brucite, 7.5–11.5 for hydrotalcite) and conductivity (3.4 mS cm⁻¹ and 8.6 mS cm⁻¹ respectively) with a Thermo Scientific Orion multiparameter (Star A329).

steps.title: Calculate electrical operating cost
steps.instruction:
Use the following equations:
EOC = ECC + EMC
ECC = UED × EEP
EMC = (UEM_Al × EMP_Al) + (UEM_AZ31 × EMP_AZ31)
UED = I × ∫₀ᵗ U dt (where I = 5 mA, U is cell voltage, t is operation time in h)
Given: EMP_Al = 2.7 USD kg⁻¹, EMP_AZ31 = 25 USD kg⁻¹, EEP = 0.315 USD kWh⁻¹, UED = 0.588 kWh kg⁻¹, and the material demand fractions UEM_Al = 1/3, UEM_AZ31 = 2/3. Compute EOC in USD kg⁻¹.

description: Layered double hydroxides (LDHs) also know like hydrotalcites, have attracted enormous interest due to their many potential applications like anion exchangers, base catalysts, metal oxides precursors, PVC additives and drug delivery [1]. These LDHs materials can be describe using this general formula:MII1-xMIIIxOH2Ax/nn-∙mH2OWhere MII represents divalent cations such as Mg2+, Fe2+, Ni2+, Cu2+, Co2+, Mn2+, .Zn2+ or Cd2+, MIII denotes trivalent cations like Al3+, Cr3+, .Ga3+ or Fe3+, An- is a n- valent exchangeable anion like CO32-, SO42-, Cl-, NO3-, organic and inorganic anions, x varies between approximately 0.25 to 0.33 and m is the content of intercalated-water [2]. The major advantage of LDHs for their functional applications is their flexible composition, i.e., the ratio and nature of the divalent and trivalent metal cations and the varied interlayer structure through the substitution of many different anions in the interlayer of LDHs [3,4]. As a result, several types of hydrotalcites are used in various applications, depending on their composition, crystallinity, thermal stability and other physicochemical properties [[5], [6], [7]]. LDHs is generally synthesized under very strict experimental conditions in order to avoid chemical segregations and improve homogeneities, but the most common synthesis methods are co-precipitation at constant or variable pH [6]. The Urea decomposition method by hydrolyzing urea, using hexamethylene tetramine, creates an alkaline environment and well-crystallized LDHs. Another popular method is the Reconstruction from oxide generated by calcining LDHs, taking advantage of “memory effect” also allows the intercalation of any desired anion, such as biomedical or hazardous anions [[8], [9], [10]]. In general, there still exist some technological-economic problems involved in LDHs preparation. Although, the high maintenance costs and space requirements are drawbacks of the process [11,12].
